In other words, it is wrong even to say that God could possibly do wrong.
Al-Naẓẓām therefore concluded that God cannot have the power to do evil, because saying that He has such power means admitting that evil could possibly come from Him.
At this point, however, al-Naẓẓām partly moved the discussion away from the specifically Muʿtazilite idea of justice and toward another idea: divine grace and care for human beings.
He said that God can do only what He knows will benefit people in their worldly lives.

As for the next life, God cannot be described as having the power to increase the punishment of the people of Hell or to reduce it. Nor can He reduce the happiness of the people of Paradise or remove anyone from Paradise. None of these things lies within His power.
Muʿtazilite writings sometimes used this kind of language—that God acts for what benefits human beings—to explain the idea of divine grace.
By this they meant that God knows from eternity what each person will choose to do, but may, through His grace, help those who choose the good.

Bishr ibn al-Muʿtamir explained the idea by saying that if God knows that a particular person would become a believer if allowed to remain alive, then keeping that person alive is better for them than allowing them to die as an unbeliever.
This is essentially what al-Naẓẓām was pointing toward in the argument above.
But in another statement he returns directly to the distinctively Muʿtazilite idea of justice.
He says that if a child were standing at the edge of Hell, God would not have the power to throw the child in, although the child would have the power to throw himself in.
Here the issue is no longer divine grace. It is Muʿtazilite justice itself, where the limits of divine power are set by the human being’s freedom to choose.
Another group of Muʿtazilites objected to al-Naẓẓām.

They argued that if God has no power to do evil or commit sin, then He would be naturally compelled to do what He does rather than freely choosing it. A being truly described as powerful, they argued, must be able either to act or not to act. Al-Naẓẓām’s position removes that choice from divine power.

What you say about power applies equally to what you yourselves say about action. You say that it is impossible for God to do evil even though He has the power to do it. So what is the difference between our two positions?
If it is impossible for God actually to do evil, whether or not He theoretically has the power to do so, then in either case God does not have a real choice between doing evil and not doing it.
The Muʿtazilites tried to solve it by turning to another idea: divine wisdom.
God, they said, is unquestionably wise, and a wise being does nothing without wisdom.

God’s wisdom in commanding human beings to obey and avoid wrongdoing lies in choosing what is best for them. And what is best for human beings requires that they have the power to perform their own actions.
God therefore gave them reason, through which they can understand good and evil and choose between different actions.
Human power and human choice thus fall within a permanent and consistent law of divine wisdom.
The Baghdad Muʿtazilites took this argument further than the Basra Muʿtazilites.

According to the Baghdad school, divine wisdom requires that everything that happens to a person in this life—misfortune, pain, or their opposites—and everything that happens in the next life—happiness or punishment—must be what is good, or best, for that person.

Poverty may therefore be better for one person than wealth, while the opposite may be true for another. Illness may be better than health, or health better than illness. Even remaining forever in Hell might be better for someone than remaining forever in Paradise.
This way of handling the problem seems to involve a partial return to the traditionalist outlook that the Muʿtazilites had opposed.
It also seems to move away from the rationalist approach they defended so firmly in many of the great intellectual battles of their history.
The Basra Muʿtazilites came less close to traditionalism and moved less far from their rationalism.

They agreed that divine wisdom led God, out of generosity, to create human beings and place them under the obligations of religious law. But they also held that this same wisdom required God to remove the obstacles that prevent human beings from achieving what is best for them.
And what is “best” can be defined here quite clearly: human beings must be able to understand through reason and must have the power to act.
Because they have this capacity, they must then receive reward for obedience and punishment for wrongdoing.

Abū al-Hudhayl al-ʿAllāf, one of the leading figures of the Basra school, explained this idea of “what is best” by saying that God has the power to do something less than the best, but does not do so. Instead, He does what is better.

“To do something less good when something better could be done would be corruption. If God did what was less good and withheld what was better, both things would be corrupt. Nor can it be said that God could have done something better than what He actually did. If He could have done something better, then doing the better thing would have been more fitting. God does not leave aside what is best, because what is best is what is most fitting for Him.”

In another passage, also preserved by al-Ashʿarī, Abū al-Hudhayl says that God has the power to commit injustice and wrongdoing, and to act unjustly and wrongly, but does not do so. It is impossible for Him to do so in practice because such acts could come only from deficiency, and deficiency cannot be attributed to God.

God did not create human beings because He needed them. He created them because creating them was wise. He intended their benefit and is not miserly. It is therefore impossible for Him to leave aside what is best and do something inferior instead.
Yet although al-ʿAllāf clearly affirms in theory that God has the power to do less than what is best, and even has the power to act unjustly, he ends up denying this power in practice.

The issue becomes especially clear when the following question is raised: if God has given a human being the power to perform a certain act—an act of injustice, sin, or evil, for example—does God still retain the power to perform that same act?
On this question, al-ʿAllāf gives an explicit answer.
He denies that God retains such power, relying on an old philosophical principle:
“It is impossible for one and the same act to lie within the power of two agents.”

In general, then, the Basra and Baghdad Muʿtazilites differed in how they tried to escape the difficulty their theory of justice and power had created for them. But they agreed on the essential point: human freedom of action is the central content of justice.

They therefore agreed that God does not commit evil or sinful acts, whether He theoretically has the power to do so, as most Muʿtazilites held, or does not have that power at all, as al-Naẓẓām’s school argued.
Their determination to defend freedom of the human will went very far.

Bishr ibn al-Muʿtamir expressed the point by saying that God is not the ally of an obedient person at the moment that person is performing the act of obedience, and is not the enemy of an unbeliever at the moment that person is committing unbelief.
God becomes the ally of the obedient person only after the act of obedience has taken place, and becomes the enemy of the unbeliever only after the act of unbelief has taken place.
What Bishr means is that God’s will does not enter into the person’s act of obedience or unbelief while the act itself is happening.
God judges the obedient person only after the act of obedience has occurred, and judges the unbeliever only after the act of unbelief has occurred.
In other words, whether an action is good or bad, it happens only because the human being freely chooses and wills it.
Reward for obedience and punishment for wrongdoing are therefore nothing more than God’s judgment about what a person deserves for something they themselves freely chose to do.
B — The Opposition to Limiting Divine Power
As we have said, the Muʿtazilites placed themselves in a difficult position before the wider Sunni public when they developed their distinctive theory of justice.
They faced fierce opposition. Many traditionalists went so far as to accuse them of abandoning Islam itself.
The central idea behind this opposition was that God’s power is absolute and unlimited, while His will includes everything and is itself contained by nothing.
God creates every action and every event.

Human beings do not create any of their own actions, because to say that they do would be to place human power alongside God’s power. This, the critics argued, would mean introducing a second creator.
For this reason, the Muʿtazilites were compared in their own age to the Zoroastrians, who were accused of believing in two creators.
This comparison went back to the first appearance of the Qadarites.

Opponents of the view that human actions are free from divine predestination deliberately called the earliest supporters of human freedom “Qadarites” so that they could apply to them the reported saying of the Prophet:
“The Qadarites are the Zoroastrians of this community.”
We discussed this earlier when examining the origins of the issue.
The Ashʿarites found in the Muʿtazilite idea of justice—and especially in the claim that human power limits divine power—fertile ground for attacking Muʿtazilite beliefs.
Sometimes they went so far that they interpreted Muʿtazilite statements in ways the Muʿtazilites themselves did not intend.

One of the clearest examples appears in al-Isfarāyīnī’s al-Tabṣīr fī al-Dīn (p. 48). Al-Isfarāyīnī, one of the major Ashʿarite writers, pushes the Muʿtazilite position much further than it actually goes.
He says that the Muʿtazilite belief that human beings create their own acts leads to the conclusion:

“That every one of them—like a gnat, mosquito, bee, ant, worm, or fish—is a creator who creates his own acts; that God does not create their acts and has no power over any of what they do; and that He has no power over anything done by all the animals. They”—the Muʿtazilites—“thus established countless creators beyond number. They removed the actions of animals from God’s power while placing no corresponding restriction on describing Him as powerful. In this way they prepared the road to dualism.”
We do not know where al-Isfarāyīnī got the idea that the Muʿtazilite teaching about human beings creating their own acts could be extended to animals.
Even the Arabic term ʿibād—“God’s human servants”—is not normally used in Arabic terminology or texts to refer to animals.

Nor is there anything in the statements of Muʿtazilite thinkers on this issue that suggests their discussion of human actions also included animal actions or that the creation of actions extended beyond human beings.
It is especially strange to accuse the Muʿtazilites of dualism, or even of preparing the way for belief in two creators.
These were the very thinkers who defended belief in God’s absolute oneness so intensely that the history of Arab-Islamic thought came to call them the People of Divine Unity.
Their concern for the purity of this belief led them to investigate the divine attributes in a new theoretical way that had not existed before them.
It also led them into some of their fiercest intellectual battles, especially against those they regarded as dualists and against those who described God in human or bodily terms.
This commitment was so obvious that many of their fiercest historical opponents admitted it, and modern opponents have done the same.
One contemporary Ashʿarite researcher, for example, admits that the Muʿtazilites’ special theory of justice was:

“A branch of their theory of divine unity. They denied attributes of God in order to keep Him free from resemblance to created beings, and in the same way they keep Him free from injustice so that He does not resemble created beings in committing injustice.”
Yet after making this admission, the same researcher gives another criticism that also seems unfair.
“By affirming justice alone, they truly tore divine unity apart. In the question of justice, God is not alone in His action. Human beings share with Him in cosmic action.”
But the Muʿtazilites did not treat justice differently from the other divine attributes.
Their denial of separate divine attributes, understood in the special way they explained it, applied to every quality Muslims attributed to God.
The second is that the Muʿtazilite texts we quoted earlier do not strip God of power over everything.
They make God the one who gives human beings the power to act.
Human power over human actions therefore remains contained within God’s power. It does not stand beside it as a partner “in cosmic action,” as this researcher claims.

If we also take into account what the Muʿtazilites said about divine grace, divine wisdom, and God doing what is best for human beings, it becomes clear that they were extremely careful in their arguments not to undermine the foundations of Islamic metaphysics as a whole.
The truth is that the Muʿtazilites never left the Islamic metaphysical framework.
What they tried to do, from within that framework, was something else.
With great courage, persistence, intellectual honesty, and openness, they tried to raise the human being above the level of a mere thing, or a purely mechanical object.
They tried to give human reason the highest place that their philosophical and social awareness could reach under the historical conditions of their society and their age.
